Tiny Tools for Tidy Notebooks

Last week I spent an afternoon building a small helper that renames the cells of a notebook so that they sort in the order they were written. The idea is simple, but the details turned out to be more interesting than I expected, so here are my notes on how it works.

The helper walks every cell, reads its first comment line and turns that into a slug. Cells without a comment get a numbered placeholder so nothing is ever left unnamed, which matters when two people edit the same notebook on different days.

def slugify(line: str) -> str:
    words = [w for w in line.lower().split() if w.isalnum()]
    return "-".join(words[:6]) or "cell"

The second half of the tool checks for collisions. If two cells produce the same slug it appends a counter, starting at two, because the first cell keeps the plain name. I wrote a handful of tests for this part, since off-by-one mistakes in counters are exactly the sort of thing that sneaks past a quick manual check.

def unique(slugs: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    seen: dict[str, int] = {}
    out = []
    for slug in slugs:
        seen[slug] = seen.get(slug, 0) + 1
        out.append(slug if seen[slug] == 1 else f"{slug}-{seen[slug]}")
    return out

Finally, the tool writes the notebook back with the original formatting intact. Preserving whitespace was the fiddliest requirement, because the JSON writer I started with reflowed every long line and produced diffs that were far larger than the change itself.

I have been using it for a week now and the notebooks in my archive are noticeably easier to navigate. The next step is to teach it about cell tags, so that the slug can carry a hint about whether the cell is setup, analysis or output.
